story.title: Karoline Leavitt to Depart as White House Press Secretary, Succession Speculation Begins
story.summary: Karoline Leavitt is set to leave her position as White House Press Secretary at the end of the month, as announced by President Trump. Leavitt, who recently returned from maternity leave, cited a desire to spend more time with her family as the reason for her departure. Speculation is already underway regarding potential candidates to succeed her, although the White House has not confirmed any names.

event_overview.title: About White House Press Secretary
event_overview.subject: White House Press Secretary
event_overview.summary: This event concerns a planned leadership change in the White House Press Secretary’s Office, the office that communicates the president’s activities and agenda to the media. Karoline Leavitt has held the role during President Donald Trump’s second administration; the reported departure sets up a White House decision on her successor rather than a Senate-confirmed vacancy.

facts.label: Role and institution
facts.value: The White House describes the Press Secretary’s Office as part of the Executive Office of the President; the press secretary provides media briefings on the president’s activities and agenda.

facts.label: Officeholder and start date
facts.value: Karoline Leavitt’s public financial disclosure identifies her White House position as Press Secretary and lists January 20, 2025, as her appointment date. A White House announcement also identified her as an Assistant to the President and Press Secretary.

facts.label: Stated communications function
facts.value: The White House Press Office works with media organizations worldwide, while the Office of Communications plans and advances the president’s core messaging; the press secretary is the administration’s principal public briefing official within that structure.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the announced departure and immediate discussion of possible succession, not every White House briefing, personnel development, or any later formal successor appointment.

explore_lenses.label: What changes for Leavitt after August?
explore_lenses.title: She is leaving the podium, not Trump’s orbit
explore_lenses.summary: Leavitt’s departure ends her daily White House press-secretary role at the end of August, but Trump says he expects her to remain politically involved as an outside adviser. Her own statement frames the decision as a family-work balance choice after returning from maternity leave.

claims.text: Trump said Leavitt will leave the press-secretary job at the end of August to spend more time with her children and family, while remaining one of his “top outside advisors.”

Leavitt said that the constant demands of the press-secretary job prevented her from being the mother she wants to be to her two young children; she described the decision as bittersweet and said she would remain an advocate for MAGA and the Republican Party.
The announcement came less than a month after Leavitt’s first briefing following maternity leave; ABC reported that she gave birth to her second child in May.

explore_lenses.label: How will the next press secretary be chosen?
explore_lenses.title: The choice is expected to be presidential
explore_lenses.summary: There is no announced succession process or nominee. The available legal framework gives the President broad authority to appoint White House Office employees, so the central outstanding decision is Trump’s selection rather than a known Senate-confirmation timetable.

claims.text: The White House had not identified a successor or said when a decision would be made; TIME reported that it referred questions about candidates to Trump’s and Leavitt’s public posts and said no decision had been made.
Federal law authorizes the President to appoint and set pay for White House Office employees without regard to other laws regulating federal employment and compensation.

The statute cited does not set out a press-secretary-specific Senate confirmation step; this supports an inference that the vacancy can be filled through White House personnel selection rather than the Cabinet-nomination process.

During Leavitt’s maternity leave, Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent were among officials who held briefing-room press conferences, showing the administration has used multiple stand-ins rather than a single publicly designated interim.

story_report.summary: White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt will leave the post at the end of August, President Donald Trump said, citing her wish to spend more time with her family. Trump said she would remain one of his top outside advisers, though the parameters of that role have not been specified. The White House has not named a replacement or set a timetable for choosing one, leaving the administration’s briefing-room leadership unsettled ahead of her departure.

sections.heading: Leavitt Cites Demands of Motherhood
sections.body: Leavitt recently returned from maternity leave following the birth of her second child in May; her first briefing after leave was less than a month before the announcement. She said the constant demands of serving as press secretary had prevented her from being the mother she wants to be to her two young children. Calling the decision bittersweet, Leavitt said she would remain an advocate for MAGA and the Republican Party.

sections.heading: White House Faces Press Office Transition
sections.body: The White House said no decision had been made on Leavitt’s successor and referred questions about candidates to public posts by Trump and Leavitt. During her maternity leave, Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent were among officials who held briefing-room press conferences, rather than a single publicly designated interim spokesperson. Federal law authorizes the president to appoint White House Office employees and set their pay; the cited statute does not specify a press-secretary confirmation step.

unresolved.text: The scope, compensation and start date of Leavitt’s proposed outside-adviser role have not been specified.
It remains unconfirmed whether the White House will appoint an interim spokesperson, whether Leavitt will hold a final briefing, and who will oversee routine briefing decisions after her departure.

related_stories.title: Zambians Vote in Presidential Election Amid Economic Concerns
related_stories.summary: Zambians voted on Thursday in a presidential election that tests the economic reforms of incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema. Approximately 8 million registered voters also selected members of Parliament and local councilors. Vote counting is currently underway, with results expected on Monday.

related_stories.title: Nigel Farage Wins Clacton By-Election Against Count Binface
related_stories.summary: Nigel Farage, leader of the Reform UK party, won the Clacton by-election with 63% of the vote, defeating novelty candidate Count Binface, who received 27%. The election was criticized by major parties as a stunt, and Farage reportedly skipped the vote count due to security concerns following a credible threat against him. This election was triggered by Farage's resignation from the seat a month prior.

related_stories.title: Zambia Halts Vote Counting Amid Violence and Ballot Theft Reports
related_stories.summary: Zambia's electoral commission has suspended the counting of votes from the recent presidential and parliamentary elections due to violence directed at polling staff and reports of stolen marked ballots. The commission plans to reassess the situation within 24 hours. The main opposition candidate has expressed concern over the delays in the vote counting process.

related_stories.title: Kennedy Center Board Votes to Reinstate Trump's Name Amid Legal Challenges
related_stories.summary: The Kennedy Center's board of trustees has voted to restore Donald Trump's name on the building's facade, despite a previous court order mandating its removal. This decision also includes plans for a two-year renovation of the main building while keeping a smaller addition open. The move may lead to further legal disputes regarding the center's naming and future.
